transcript.text: This morning, I received a protocol update from the regional poison center. Their current protocol recommends that hydroxocobalamin kits be immediately available in the satellite emergency department for suspected smoke-inhalation exposures, rather than retrieved from the main pharmacy. This is a critical timing consideration — in cases of cyanide toxicity from smoke inhalation, every minute of delay in administration can be the difference between life and death. Retrieval from the main pharmacy would introduce unacceptable delays, which is why the kits need to be stocked directly in the satellite ED.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: Thank you, Dr. Moreno. Now let me share the manufacturer requirements I confirmed with the distributor today. The manufacturer supplies these hydroxocobalamin kits only in cases of six, requires storage at 2-8 degrees Celsius (refrigerated), and requires a documented staff-use training session to be completed before the first kit can be placed into service. These three requirements will directly impact our decisions on quantity, storage arrangement, and staff readiness. For example, if we stock in the satellite ED, we'll need refrigeration capable of maintaining 2-8 degrees Celsius at that location, and we'll need to plan and document a training session for ED staff before any kits go live. The case-of-six minimum also means our quantity decision should account for that increment.
